Organisation Learning Plan: Hazira gas terminal release and fire, 2020

Site leadership and the HSE function, planning the learning cascade · Hazira 2020 · 2020-09-24 · run 2020-09-24-hazira-gas-release-fire · generated 2026-10-22

About 13 min read

Learning purposes: not a statutory document. Draft learnings from a ProbeMatrix investigation export; validate them before adoption. · Learnings drafted by an AI agent from AI-assisted findings

Review: draft · Classification: internal · Version 1.0

Draft because: the investigation status is in progress; no finding is marked as edited by a person

Data quality and limits

  • Draft learnings from an unreviewed analysis: the export's Investigation Status is in_progress and no finding is marked as edited by a person, so this pack stays a draft until the investigation is completed and reviewed.

Bottom line

  • Mechanical Maintenance owns four priority-1 learnings (specification, test, independent check, repeat failures) and is the first function to brief.
  • Operations & Control Room and Emergency Planning & Command own the isolation learnings: hand-only valves, no isolation criteria and no delegated authority.
  • Every one of the eleven priority-1 learnings reaches tiers T1 to T4, so frontline, supervisors, managers and site leaders all have something to change.
  • Deliver site-leadership-coach and supervisor-coach first, then the function and frontline packs, then top management, the board and auditors.

Where the learning sits

3

The findings concentrate in two clusters: Mechanical Maintenance (F02, 194 findings) and Operations & Control Room (F01, 170). Engineering, Design, Documents & MOC (F07, 84), HSE, Process Safety & Audit (F11, 80) and Asset Integrity (F05, 70) follow [; ; ; ; ].

Language check JC8 accepted: counts are from PMLC facts for this export

Most of the learning is for supervision and the organisation: 308 of the 436 findings sit at levels 3 and 4. By tier, function managers (T3, 247 findings), frontline (T1, 227) and first-line supervisors (T2, 219) are most involved; site leadership holds 63 findings and top management one [; ].

Language check JC8 accepted: counts are from PMLC facts and the profile for this export

Each tier section below lists up to six of that tier's priority-1 learnings, the ones with the most findings in the tier first; the full set, with every tier's message, is in the Learnings Register and the organisation learning map. Eighty-seven role strings are not yet placed in a tier (T9), so tier counts are a lower bound [].

What the frontline (T1) must learn

6

If you cannot confirm a seal or gasket matches the specification for a pressure part, stop and ask for the spec. Do not fit 'what we normally use'. Owner: F02 Mechanical Maintenance

If the original specification for a pressure-boundary part is lost and no role owns re-establishing it, maintainers will fit whatever part is to hand, and the substitute becomes normal practice, because the job has to be done and nothing in the system says 'stop'.

After any work that opens a pressure boundary, ask: what test proves this joint, and who witnessed it? Write the answer on the job record. Owner: F02 Mechanical Maintenance

If no procedure defines how a high-pressure joint is tested before return to service, crews will use the quickest available check (pressurising to operating pressure), and a weak joint will pass, because operating pressure does not prove the joint against the pressures it must withstand.

A flameproof fitting with a missing bolt or open cover is not flameproof. Report it and make it safe the same shift. Owner: F03 Electrical Maintenance

If electrical maintenance in hazardous areas responds to breakdowns instead of inspecting explosion-protected equipment, defects that do not stop the equipment working (missing bolts, open enclosures) stay in service until a release finds them.

Ask for practice on the emergencies you are expected to handle. If you have never practised one, tell your supervisor. Owner: F01 Operations & Control Room

If no qualification is defined for control-room operators, people are assigned to emergency duty after general training only, and a rare, time-critical event becomes their first practice, because rostering fills posts with whoever is available.

Treat a gas alarm as late news: the release has already started. Act on it as confirmed until proved otherwise. Owner: F04 Instrumentation, Control & Calibration

If fire and gas detection only lights an annunciator, every protective action depends on people noticing, verifying and deciding, which takes minutes to tens of minutes, because the system was designed to inform rather than act.

If you are fixing the same fault again, say so on the job record. That note is what starts a root-cause review. Owner: F02 Mechanical Maintenance

If nothing in the maintenance system counts repeat failures on the same item, each failure is fixed as if it were the first, and the same inadequate repair is repeated until it fails in the worst conditions.

What first-line supervisors (T2) must learn

6

Before signing off pressure-boundary work, check the part against a written specification. No spec means no sign-off. Owner: F02 Mechanical Maintenance

If the original specification for a pressure-boundary part is lost and no role owns re-establishing it, maintainers will fit whatever part is to hand, and the substitute becomes normal practice, because the job has to be done and nothing in the system says 'stop'.

Do not roster anyone alone on emergency duty who has not passed the emergency-response assessment for that unit. Owner: F01 Operations & Control Room

If no qualification is defined for control-room operators, people are assigned to emergency duty after general training only, and a rare, time-critical event becomes their first practice, because rostering fills posts with whoever is available.

Do not accept equipment back from maintenance without a recorded leak/pressure test to the written test pressure. Owner: F02 Mechanical Maintenance

If no procedure defines how a high-pressure joint is tested before return to service, crews will use the quickest available check (pressurising to operating pressure), and a weak joint will pass, because operating pressure does not prove the joint against the pressures it must withstand.

Know the isolation trigger and the valves for each release scenario on your unit. Do not wait for the call chain to isolate. Owner: F09b Emergency Planning & Command

If an emergency plan names a release scenario but not who may isolate, and on what criteria, isolation waits for escalation up the chain, because people at the scene reasonably believe they need permission to shut in a major supply.

Include Ex-equipment checks (bolts, covers, glands) in area rounds and record them by item, not as a group. Owner: F03 Electrical Maintenance

If electrical maintenance in hazardous areas responds to breakdowns instead of inspecting explosion-protected equipment, defects that do not stop the equipment working (missing bolts, open enclosures) stay in service until a release finds them.

Raise a root-cause request when the same item fails twice in a year. Owner: F02 Mechanical Maintenance

If nothing in the maintenance system counts repeat failures on the same item, each failure is fixed as if it were the first, and the same inadequate repair is repeated until it fails in the worst conditions.

What function managers (T3) must learn

6

Write isolation and stoppage criteria, valve lists and delegated authority into the emergency plan for every release scenario. Owner: F09b Emergency Planning & Command

If an emergency plan names a release scenario but not who may isolate, and on what criteria, isolation waits for escalation up the chain, because people at the scene reasonably believe they need permission to shut in a major supply.

Find every pressure-boundary item with no specification on file and re-establish it (OEM, reverse engineering or an engineered substitute). Owner: F02 Mechanical Maintenance

If the original specification for a pressure-boundary part is lost and no role owns re-establishing it, maintainers will fit whatever part is to hand, and the substitute becomes normal practice, because the job has to be done and nothing in the system says 'stop'.

List emergency isolation valves that are local-only and assess for each whether a release would deny access. Owner: F01 Operations & Control Room

If the valves that stop a release can only be operated at the valve, they will be unreachable in exactly the event they exist for, because a large release fills the area around them.

Run a monthly repeat-failure report from the CMMS and assign a root-cause analysis to each bad actor. Owner: F02 Mechanical Maintenance

If nothing in the maintenance system counts repeat failures on the same item, each failure is fixed as if it were the first, and the same inadequate repair is repeated until it fails in the worst conditions.

Define a control-room qualification (knowledge, simulator scenarios, assessment, refresher interval). Owner: F01 Operations & Control Room

If no qualification is defined for control-room operators, people are assigned to emergency duty after general training only, and a rare, time-critical event becomes their first practice, because rostering fills posts with whoever is available.

Define 'replacement not in kind' with examples (seals, gaskets, materials) and make it trigger MOC. Owner: F07 Engineering, Design, Documents & MOC

If a management-of-change procedure is published but never triggered, changes in parts, materials and pipework happen without risk review, because people do not recognise a 'like-for-unlike' replacement as a change.

What site leadership (T4) must learn

6

Give shift crews standing written authority to isolate and shut down on defined criteria, and back them when they do. Owner: F09b Emergency Planning & Command

If an emergency plan names a release scenario but not who may isolate, and on what criteria, isolation waits for escalation up the chain, because people at the scene reasonably believe they need permission to shut in a major supply.

Fund remote-operated (and where justified, automatic) emergency isolation for inventories that can produce a large vapour cloud. Owner: F01 Operations & Control Room

If the valves that stop a release can only be operated at the valve, they will be unreachable in exactly the event they exist for, because a large release fills the area around them.

Track the number of MOCs raised per month; zero over a long period means the system is not being used. Owner: F07 Engineering, Design, Documents & MOC

If a management-of-change procedure is published but never triggered, changes in parts, materials and pipework happen without risk review, because people do not recognise a 'like-for-unlike' replacement as a change.

Require that every shift has at least one qualified emergency-competent person in each control room. Owner: F01 Operations & Control Room

If no qualification is defined for control-room operators, people are assigned to emergency duty after general training only, and a rare, time-critical event becomes their first practice, because rostering fills posts with whoever is available.

Approve and fund F&G voting logic with automatic executive action for major-release areas. Owner: F04 Instrumentation, Control & Calibration

If fire and gas detection only lights an annunciator, every protective action depends on people noticing, verifying and deciding, which takes minutes to tens of minutes, because the system was designed to inform rather than act.

Give one named function ownership of pressure-part specifications and of approving any substitute. Owner: F02 Mechanical Maintenance

If the original specification for a pressure-boundary part is lost and no role owns re-establishing it, maintainers will fit whatever part is to hand, and the substitute becomes normal practice, because the job has to be done and nothing in the system says 'stop'.

What top management and the board (T5) must learn

5

Ask for assurance that legacy (pre-2000) pressure equipment has current part specifications and controlled spares. Owner: F02 Mechanical Maintenance

If the original specification for a pressure-boundary part is lost and no role owns re-establishing it, maintainers will fit whatever part is to hand, and the substitute becomes normal practice, because the job has to be done and nothing in the system says 'stop'.

Ask for evidence that MOC is in active use at each site, not only that a procedure exists. Owner: F07 Engineering, Design, Documents & MOC

If a management-of-change procedure is published but never triggered, changes in parts, materials and pipework happen without risk review, because people do not recognise a 'like-for-unlike' replacement as a change.

Ask whether every site's emergency plan says who may isolate, on what criteria, without calling up. Owner: F09b Emergency Planning & Command

If an emergency plan names a release scenario but not who may isolate, and on what criteria, isolation waits for escalation up the chain, because people at the scene reasonably believe they need permission to shut in a major supply.

Ask for a fleet-wide inventory of local-only emergency isolation valves on major hazard sites. Owner: F01 Operations & Control Room

If the valves that stop a release can only be operated at the valve, they will be unreachable in exactly the event they exist for, because a large release fills the area around them.

Ask for control-room competence assurance (qualified share by site) as a standing board metric. Owner: F01 Operations & Control Room

If no qualification is defined for control-room operators, people are assigned to emergency duty after general training only, and a rare, time-critical event becomes their first practice, because rostering fills posts with whoever is available.

Strength of fixes

2

Of the register's 44 recommendations, 24 (55%) sit above the administrative tier: 20 engineering, 2 substitution and 2 elimination. The other 20 are administrative or training. Stronger fixes are missing for two priority-1 learnings: the switch from locating to isolating (LR-08) and control-room competence (LR-12) have administrative and training fixes only, and the register explains why for each [; ; ; ].

Evidence trail

FND-91B45FF9
Substitute O-ring gaskets without OEM specification or quality control · L1 · rating 4. Locally-sourced O-rings routinely substituted for lost OEM gasket specs without quality control - normalized practice over 22+ months with three applications on failed meter.
FND-FD617187
Maintenance Team - No Hydro-Test Requirement Ignored · L1 · rating 4. Maintenance team skipped mandatory hydrostatic test after gasket replacement on 18-Sep-2020, ignoring fundamental pressure boundary integrity verification requirement.
FND-F8C125D5
Pressure-boundary maintenance ordered without independent QC/inspection manning · L3 · rating 4. The gasket replacement job was authorised without any independent QC, inspection, or permit-verification manning, leaving the substitute O-ring and omitted hydrotest wholly unchecked.
FND-71D631C1
Recurrent gasket failure pattern on 310FT01 not root-caused or corrected · L3 · rating 4. Three gasket replacements in 22 months on meter 310FT01 were not escalated as a chronic reliability problem; the same inadequate repair was repeated until the fourth failure caused the leak.
FND-4C645CB5
Emergency isolation MOVs not configured for remote operation from the control room · L2 · rating 4. MOV 54 and other Gas Terminal emergency isolation valves were available only for local operation and were not remote-operable from the control room.
FND-314D34C5
Control Room Operators - DMP Isolation Decision Criteria · L1 · rating 4. Operators unaware that DMP lacked isolation decision criteria for major leaks, causing them to default to physical verification and multi-layer escalation instead of immediate isolation.
FND-23139BF9
No accountable owner or recorded authority for gasket material specification and procurement · L4 · rating 4. No organizational role owned the meter gasket specification, procurement quality control, or the authority to approve the substitution from OEM rectangular-slot gasket to locally procured O-ring.
FND-82761CC5
No delegated authority or criteria for emergency isolation in DMP and night-shift structure · L4 · rating 4. The DMP/ERDMP omitted isolation criteria and no standing authority existed below Plant Manager to close MOV 54, forcing a 46-minute escalation instead of immediate isolation.
FND-B440C1BF
Unassessed program risk of O-ring substitution for OEM rectangular-slot gasket · L4 · rating 4. Locally purchased O-rings replaced lost OEM rectangular-slot gaskets as regular practice without specification, QC, MOC, or any recorded authority.
FND-A2048FB8
Hazardous O-ring substitution practice left uncorrected across multiple maintenance events · L3 · rating 4. Operations management allowed the locally-sourced O-ring substitution to continue as regular practice without specification or QC, through three gasket replacements in 22 months.
FND-8083ECAC
MOC formal risk assessment not applied to the OEM-to-O-ring gasket substitution · L3 · rating 4. The O-ring-for-OEM-gasket substitution was never processed through the Plant's MOC risk assessment, which had not been applied to any change since 2018, leaving the non-conforming seal unevaluated.
FND-303495E9
Self-safety audit checklist generic and not plant-specific; approved manuals/SOPs unavailable · L2 · rating 3. The self-safety audit used a generic non-plant-specific checklist, and approved manuals/SOPs were unavailable.
FND-47B1702F
2017 pipeline thickness-loss findings left without corrective action for three years · L3 · rating 3. Significant thickness losses identified in 2017 received no corrective action plan for three years despite a formal recommendation.
FND-F7FE8463
Management of Change policy not implemented since 2018, allowing unapproved material substitution · L4 · rating 4. The MOC SOP existed since Aug-2016 but was not applied at all after 2018, so the O-ring material substitution was never subjected to change review.
FND-2A77BAFB
External audit recommendation extensions without competent-authority approval · L4 · rating 2. Twelve external-audit recommendations remained overdue on extensions to 30-Apr-2021 for which no Director Offshore approval existed, breaking the formal accountability chain for closing findings.

EVD-3932
document: Plant organogram — night-shift authority chain reconstructed from witness statements (rows 1-7) and the committee's document review (p.18). Authority chain: perimeter (CISF Constable A) -> CCTV CR (CISF SI C) -> Gas Terminal CR (CE-P) -> GSP/LPG Shift In-charge (DGM-P) -> Overall Shift In-charge / SIC (GM-P) -> Resident Engineer (GM-P) + Head Operations (CGM-P) -> Plant Manager / CIC (GGM). Critical structural observation: NO role between Shift In-charge and Plant Manager has standing authority to close MOV 54 (or any other emergency-isolation valve) without telephoning up the chain — confirmed by the committee finding (p.26) that "MOVs are provided in the gas terminal station for local operations but they are not having remote operation from control room during emergency." The Overall Shift In-charge had to physically reach Gas Terminal Gate at ~02:35 and then "instructed closure" (row 7) — the operator at Gas Terminal Gate could not act unilaterally. Directly implicates the 46-minute first-detection-to-first-isolation gap. The escalation hierarchy was not designed for time-critical hydrocarbon containment.
EVD-4052
document: On-site Disaster Management Plan (DMP) — hydrocarbon-leakage section omits isolation/stoppage decision criteria. Source records: "As per DMP On site Hazira Plant, guidelines to be followed in case of hydrocarbon leakage are included but does not include isolation/stoppage of facilities/pipelines" (p.32). Reinforced at p.27: "In ERDMP, scenario for Level 3 emergencies are taken from the plant failures. Heavy product/gas leakages from pipelines & tanks are considered but decision on isolation/closure of plant/pipelines is not mentioned." The DMP defines the scenario but not the decision: when does a hydrocarbon leak warrant unilateral pipeline isolation, and who has the authority to call it? This procedural gap directly correlates with the 46-minute response delay — personnel had no documented criterion to act on, and authority was concentrated above the shift-in-charge level (row 50). The committee's root cause #6 ("Non isolation/stoppage of 36 pipeline operation") flows from this finding.
EVD-8645
document: Lost OEM gasket specification; market-sourced O-rings used as substitutes without QC. Source records: "The meter is very old (1986) and having rectangular slot for the gasket. Original Specifications of gasket are not available, and the gaskets were not being procured from the OEMs. Instead, use of locally purchased O ring was done in its place as a regular practice. There was no specification or quality control during the purchase of the O rings. There is no record of date or authority of the decision to switch over from OEM supplied gasket to locally purchased gasket" (p.31). Six omissions documented in two sentences: lost spec, no OEM procurement, market O-ring substitution, no specification, no quality control, no documented authorisation. The committee's root cause #2 ("Use of nonstandard O ring") and #3 ("Lack of control over material sourcing") flow directly from this finding. The same governance failure underlies the absence of MOC application across the plant since 2018 (row 47).
EVD-1494
document: Meter 310FE1 gasket replacement history. Source records: "Cleaning/servicing/calibration of meters 1 & 2 was carried out on 12th & 13th Nov 2018. Afterwards, meter no.1 was cleaned on 25/02/2019 & gasket was changed. Again on 18/09/2019, gasket was changed which leaked within one year" (p.27). [Note: source references 18/09/2019 in the text but 18/09/2020 in the contextual narrative on p.31; the 2020 date is the most-recent gasket change.] Three gasket replacements in ~22 months on a 1986-vintage meter with 34 years in service: 12-Nov-2018, 25-Feb-2019, 18-Sep-2020. Recurrent sealing issues visible in the SAP record; the pattern did not trigger material/procedure review and the same locally-sourced O-ring continued in use (row 30).
EVD-0064
physical_item: Damaged retaining plate of meter 310FE1 / 310FT01 (1986-vintage 6" condensate meter, rectangular slot gasket design). Source records: "6 meter with ID 310FE1 was extensively damaged with all bolts out of the flange arrangement" (p.31) and "The condensate might have leaked from the meter 310FE1" (p.33). All retaining-plate bolts displaced; physical evidence of catastrophic flange-joint failure. Compare to 310FE2 (row 15) which had only one bolt damaged. Identified by the committee as the probable loss-of-containment source. The gasket-precondition failures (rows 29-32) explain why the joint failed.
EVD-2894
document: Pressure boundary integrity record: NO hydro test performed after 18-Sep-2020 gasket replacement. Source records: "After calibration of the meter 310FE01, the gasket was replaced on 18.09.2020. No hydro test was done after replacement of the gasket. The system was only pressurised to operating pressure (Both meters were in line) and isolated. Next day meter 310FE01 was taken on online and was in use at the time of Incident" (p.31). System pressurised only to operating pressure; standard pressure-boundary integrity test (hydro test to design pressure) not performed. The committee directly cites this as a contributing cause: "Probable cause of leak is due to use of nonstandard gasket and not testing the system to designed pressure. No standard operating procedure is in place for calibration and taking back in service of these meters which are operating at high pressures" (p.32).
EVD-0185
log_record: Meter 310FE1 returned to service ~46 hours after the 18-Sep-2020 gasket replacement. Source records: "Next day meter 310FE01 was taken on online and was in use at the time of Incident" (p.31). Replacement on 18-Sep; back online 19-Sep; in service through to incident (24-Sep). No post-maintenance pressure validation captured (row 32). SAP notification 3800419840 not closed after job completion (row 28). The committee recommendation D.2.ii at p.35 explicitly addresses the closure-review gap: "Sample checks/approval of closure of notifications by Senior Officers to be introduced".
EVD-6916
physical_item: HPMV (high-pressure mercury vapour) flame-proof lamp post with compromised integrity, identified by the committee as the probable ignition source. Source records: "three bolts on one of the flame proof lamps were missing resulting in it being open with its integrity compromised, glass case got detached from the main body and had opened out about 5 to 6 cms. The nearby fittings were found intact" (p.32). Three bolts missing; glass case opened 5-6 cm. The "nearby fittings were intact" qualifier bounds the ignition origin to this single lamp. The Zone 1 hydrocarbon area requires flame-proof integrity; that integrity was demonstrably absent on this fitting.
EVD-9999
document: Post-incident electrical preventive maintenance audit report on the 9 HPMV FLP lamps in the affected area. Source records: "Post the incident, an electrical audit of the affected area was carried out by the plant maintenance team. Considering that the audit was carried out to identify the damage to the equipment, the report is too generic and short (One page) and does not cover details of damages... the report has clubbed all nine 125 W HPMV FLP lamps together and reported 'cable burnt and fitting damaged due to heat' as status for all of them" (p.28). Single-page report; 9 lamps grouped under one status line; no per-equipment detail. Compounded by: "the electrical maintenance system is a lot more skewed towards breakdown maintenance and lays little emphasis on systematic preventive maintenance and inspection" (p.28). Even the post-incident audit was insufficient to characterise per-equipment failure mode.
EVD-0496
photograph: Post-incident electrical PM audit photographs of 9 HPMV FLP lamps (125 W each) in the metering-skid blast radius. Source describes the audit report itself: "the report has clubbed all nine 125 W HPMV FLP lamps together and reported 'cable burnt and fitting damaged due to heat' as status for all of them. However, the unique condition of one particular lamp due to the type of damage suffered by it with respect to its area of installation was not mentioned in the report" (p.28). The committee further notes "the electrical maintenance system is a lot more skewed towards breakdown maintenance and lays little emphasis on systematic preventive maintenance and inspection" (p.28). 9 of 9 fittings showed cable/fitting damage; one (row 16) had pre-existing integrity loss (3 missing bolts, glass case opened 5-6 cm) — a uniform deterioration pattern not consistent with single-event fire damage alone, indicating a systemic gap in PM coverage for FLP fittings in Zone 1/2 areas.
EVD-5634
document: Control Room Training Program — 4-day general training, no defined qualification, no simulator. Source records: "control room operations are carried out by persons inadequately trained in safety, operations, control room handling, logbook records and actions during emergency. It is informed that four days training programme is conducted for new recruitment/transfer staff which is general in nature and later the job training is carried out. Qualification of this staff is also not defined in HR/Operations Policy. Most of the staff have attended only One Basic Course since 2018" (p.30). The committee recommends (p.36): "operating staffs of control room needs to be trained for at least 1 month (preferably on simulators) before being assigning Control Room duties enabling them to handle operations & emergencies effectively" — a near-eightfold expansion of the current 4-day initial training. Three documented gaps: short initial training, no defined qualification in HR/Operations Policy, no simulator-based emergency training.
EVD-1460
witness_statement: Witness statement of Chief Engineer (Production), Gas Terminal CR, on night shift from 20:00 hrs. Source records: "At around 0220 hrs Mr. [CE] heard alarm on the annunciator panel and the same time he received a phone call from CISF SI [CCTV CR] from CCTV Control room informing him about some vapour cloud or steam leakage in Gas Terminal PH I area" (p.17). On going outside the control room he "saw the heavy cloud in phase I area" but could not approach due to dense cloud. He then informed GSP Shift I/C, LPG Shift I/C, and CFU Panel Engineer. The vapour cloud was already opaque enough by 02:20 to deny on-foot inspection of the source area. The annunciator alarm at 02:20 lagged human detection by 5 minutes — the automated detection did not pre-empt operator notification.
EVD-9220
witness_statement: Witness statement of Junior Engineer (Mechanical), Gas Terminal CR, on night shift from 20:00 hrs. Source records: "At 0220 hrs Mr. [JEA] heard alarm and phone call simultaneously. He went out of the control room and observed leakage and intense smell from Phase-I area. Visibility was very poor" (p.17). The witness joined the in-progress response rather than initiating a parallel one. Documents that secondary detection by on-shift operating personnel lagged primary CISF perimeter detection by ~5 minutes despite the witness being closer to the source. Visibility was poor enough by 02:20 to limit on-foot inspection.
EVD-8657
log_record: DCS annunciator panel record showing first alarm activation at the Gas Terminal Control Room at ~02:20 hrs. Source records: "At around 0220 hrs Mr. [CE] heard alarm on the annunciator panel" (p.17). Quantitative comparison: leak onset 02:12:50 (CCTV) -> human detection 02:15 (CISF) -> annunciator alarm 02:20. The automated detection lagged human detection by 5 minutes and lagged leak onset by ~7 minutes 10 seconds. The committee notes (p.26): "Hydrocarbon/H2S detectors are configured to Annunciator Panel for display but not in DCS for history" and "F&G detection system does not have provision for auto shut down of plant or activation of fire suppression system." The detector data is configured for display-only, not for trend/predictive alarms or auto-isolation interlocks.
EVD-3452
document: Plant layout drawings reviewed by the committee, including main plant layout and Flame & Gas detector overlay. Source records the document set: "Layout of the Plant / Layout of Plant along with F&G detectors / Layout of MCP-Gas Terminal" (p.18). F&G detection coverage exists per drawing. The critical operational implication is found at p.26: "F&G detection system does not have provision for auto shut down of plant or activation of fire suppression system" — the coverage is documented and instrumented but not interlocked to action. The committee's recommendation A.1 at p.34 explicitly calls for: "F&G detection system needs to be interlocked to automatic plant shut down and activation of fire suppression system." This is the same gap that allowed the 46-minute pre-ignition response delay.
EVD-1284
recording: CCTV frame 02:12:50 — the earliest visible vapour leakage commencement at the condensate metering skid. Source describes the frame as: "Commencement of Vapour leakage" (p.19). This timestamp defines clock-zero for the 46-minute response-delay calculation in the committee's root-cause analysis: leak onset 02:12:50 -> first physical detection 02:15 (~145s machine-to-human gap) -> first valve closure 03:01. The leak was machine-witnessed before any human notification was possible, but neither the F&G system nor the DCS produced a real-time alarm at this point because hydrocarbon detectors are configured to the annunciator panel only, and not in DCS for history (p.26).
EVD-0591
log_record: SAP Notification 3800419840 raised 17-Sep-2020 for malfunction of meter 310FE1 / 310FT01. Source records: "Notification no. 3800419840 was raised on 17/09/2020 for malfunction of meter no.1" (p.27); confirmed p.33: "SAP Notification 3800419840 dt. 17.09.2020 was raised for checking meter 1." Sequence: 14-17 Sep performance check observed jerks from meter 1; notification raised 17-Sep; gasket replaced 18-Sep; meter back online 19-Sep; incident 24-Sep. The actionable maintenance trigger preceded the incident by exactly 7 days. The corrective work executed (gasket replacement using locally-sourced O-ring without specification or QC, see row 30) was inadequate to address the underlying issue. The notification "was not closed after completion of the job" (p.27) — no supervisory closure check.
EVD-6414
log_record: Reconstructed emergency response timeline — composite of CCTV, DCS, and witness statements. Source records the timeline (Section 5, pp.9-12; Section 9, pp.18-25): leak onset 02:12:50 (CCTV) -> first physical detection 02:15 (CISF perimeter) -> CISF-internal verification via CCTV 02:18 -> Gas Terminal CR notification 02:18-02:20 -> annunciator alarm 02:20 -> shift-in-charge phone call ~02:35 -> shift-in-charge reaches gate, MOV 54 closure 03:01 -> 36" PCV closure 03:04 -> ignition 03:08:15. Two critical intervals: 46 minutes from first detection to first isolation; 8 minutes from first isolation to ignition (the cloud already in the air ignited regardless of the eventual valve closures). The committee characterises this directly: "Decision of closure of valve was taken after about 40 minutes resulting the spread of vapour cloud in increased area" (p.32). The delay magnitude is the proximate response failure pattern; its roots are in escalation design and the DMP gap (row 46).
EVD-9612
witness_statement: Witness statement of DGM (Production) - GSP Shift In-charge, called from quarters at ~02:35 hrs. Source records: "At around 0235 hrs, [DGM-GSP] received phone call from LPG Control Room and Gas Terminal control room, it was informed that heavy gas leakage near 36 metering area... [he] tried to enter the Gas Control room area but could not enter due to heavy gas smell. He informed Fire station to abstain from any vehicle movement in the plant... Further [DGM-GSP] closed the MOV 54 inlet condensate line from slug catcher to 36 metering area at about 0301 hrs. Thereafter fire occurred." (p.17). MOV 54 closure at 03:01 is 46 minutes after first physical detection (02:15) and 7 minutes before ignition (03:08:15). The shift in-charge had to physically reach Gas Terminal Gate before he could close the valve — the MOVs in the gas terminal station are not remote-operable from the control room during emergency (p.26).
EVD-7340
witness_statement: Witness statement of GM (Production) - Overall Shift In-charge / SIC, called at ~02:35 hrs. Source records that the SIC phoned Gas Terminal Control Room and "instructed to close the 36 line pressure control valve and get out of the control room. He informed LPG C/R and asked immediately informed to Resident Engineer, Head operations, Plant Manager and all other concerned" (p.17). The 36" PCV was closed at 03:04 (3 minutes after MOV 54 isolation upstream). The escalation cascaded serially up the management chain (Resident Engineer -> Head Operations -> Plant Manager) rather than via parallel auto-paging. The SIC role itself was later transferred to Head Operations on his arrival at site (p.10) — a hand-off pattern that adds time but is encoded in plant procedure.
EVD-9941
recording: CCTV sequence 02:15:35 -> 02:16:13 (5 frames over 38 seconds): vapour cloud expansion captured progressively as "vapour cloud near GT control room" (02:15:35) -> "vapour cloud on road near GT control room" (02:15:41) -> "vapour cloud in piping area" (02:15:45) -> "vapour cloud increased" (02:15:49) -> "vapour cloud intense" (02:16:13) (pp.19-21). The cloud spread from the leak source across the GT CR, road, and piping area within ~40 seconds. The flammable envelope was already established and expanding rapidly at the point of first human detection (02:15) — corroborates the operating personnel's subsequent inability to approach the source (rows 4 and 5).
EVD-2986
document: Management of Change (MOC) SOP published Aug 2016 — not implemented since 2018. Source records: "Management of Change (MOC) philosophy/SOP was published in August 2016. However, the procedure indicated in the document is not implemented while carrying out change of Low-Pressure Gas to Kribhico from Medium Pressure Gas headers in LPG Plant in 2013 & 2018. It is informed no more MOCs are implemented in the plant since 2018" (p.30). MOC SOP exists since Aug 2016. Two named uncovered changes: LP gas to Kribhico from MP headers in 2013 and 2018. ZERO MOCs issued at all since 2018 — the SOP is a paper artefact, not an active control. The same governance failure underlies the undocumented gasket substitution at the metering skid (row 30: "There is no record of date or authority of the decision to switch over from OEM supplied gasket to locally purchased gasket"). Published policy not applied in practice.
